blocks.text: In the last lesson you met the Series, a single labeled column of data, one index paired with one array of values. A DataFrame is the natural next step: it is what you get when you line up several Series side by side, all sharing that same row index. Think of a spreadsheet with named columns and numbered rows, except every column individually behaves exactly like the Series you already know. If Series felt familiar, DataFrame should feel like a small, comfortable jump rather than a brand new concept.

blocks.alt: Three Series, name, department, and salary, all sharing one row index, combining into a single DataFrame
blocks.caption: A DataFrame is several Series glued together along a shared row index.

blocks.text: 1. Introduction

Pandas is built almost entirely on two structures: the Series you already know, and the DataFrame you are about to learn. A DataFrame is a 2D labeled table. It has rows and it has columns, and both of those get labels, not just plain numeric positions. That is the biggest practical difference from a raw NumPy array, which only understands positions, never names.

items: A CSV file loaded into pandas becomes a DataFrame, one row per record, one column per field.
A SQL query result becomes a DataFrame, ready for filtering, grouping, and joining in Python.
A batch of training examples with several feature columns is usually a DataFrame before it ever becomes a NumPy array for a model.

blocks.text: Almost every real dataset you touch as an ML or AI engineer starts life as a DataFrame. Cleaning it, exploring it, and reshaping it is most of what pandas is for, and this lesson gives you the mental model that makes all of that work click into place.
2. A DataFrame Is a Dict of Aligned Series

Here is the single most useful mental model for a DataFrame, so useful that it is worth memorizing word for word: a DataFrame is a dict of Series that all share the same index. The dict keys are the column names. Each value in that dict is a full Series. And crucially, every one of those Series is lined up against the exact same row labels.
2.1 Every Column Is Literally a Series

This is not just an analogy, it is literally true in pandas. Pull any single column out of a DataFrame and you get back a real Series object, with its own index and its own values, exactly the object type you studied in the previous lesson.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Asha", "Rohit", "Meera"],
    "salary": [72000, 65000, 81000],
})

salary_column = df["salary"]
print(type(salary_column))   # <class 'pandas.core.series.Series'>
print(salary_column)

blocks.text: Nothing new is invented here. A DataFrame does not have some separate, totally different internal representation for a column. It genuinely stores each column as a Series, and reuses everything you already learned: the index, the dtype, the vectorized operations, all of it.
2.2 They All Share One Common Row Index

The second half of the mental model is just as important. All those Series inside a DataFrame are not independent, they are aligned to one shared row index. Row 0 in the name column, row 0 in the department column, and row 0 in the salary column all describe the same employee. Change the shared index and every column moves together.

blocks.title: Why this matters later
blocks.content: Once you get to merging, joining, and grouping DataFrames a few lessons from now, almost every operation is really about aligning indexes. The habit of thinking "columns are Series glued to one shared index" starts paying off immediately and keeps paying off for the rest of the pandas module.

blocks.text: You can inspect that shared index directly, and it looks exactly like the index you saw on a plain Series.

code.content:
print(df.index)
# RangeIndex(start=0, stop=3, step=1)

print(df["salary"].index)
print(df["name"].index)
# both identical to df.index

blocks.text: 3. Creating a DataFrame

There are three ways to build a DataFrame that you will run into constantly: from a dict of lists, from a list of dicts, and from a 2D NumPy array plus a list of column names. Each one fits a different situation, and it helps to recognize all three on sight.
3.1 From a Dict of Lists

This is the most common way to hand write a small DataFrame. Each dict key becomes a column name, and each dict value, a plain Python list, becomes that column full of values. Every list needs to be the same length, since they all have to line up against one shared row index.

blocks.alt: A dict of lists where each key becomes a DataFrame column name and each list becomes that column of values
blocks.caption: Dict keys become column names, dict values become column values.

code.content:
data = {
    "name": ["Asha", "Rohit", "Meera"],
    "department": ["Engineering", "Sales", "Engineering"],
    "salary": [72000, 65000, 81000],
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(df)
#     name   department  salary
# 0   Asha   Engineering  72000
# 1  Rohit         Sales  65000
# 2  Meera   Engineering  81000

blocks.text: 3.2 From a List of Dicts

This shape shows up naturally whenever your data arrives one record at a time, for example rows read out of a JSON API, one dict per response. Here each dict becomes one row, and the dict keys across all the rows become the column names.

blocks.alt: A list of dicts where each individual dict becomes one row of the resulting DataFrame
blocks.caption: Each dict in the list becomes exactly one row.

code.content:
records = [
    {"name": "Asha", "department": "Engineering", "salary": 72000},
    {"name": "Rohit", "department": "Sales", "salary": 65000},
    {"name": "Meera", "department": "Engineering", "salary": 81000},
]
df = pd.DataFrame(records)
print(df.shape)   # (3, 3), 3 rows, 3 columns

blocks.title: If a key is missing from one dict
blocks.content: Pandas does not throw an error, it just fills that cell in with NaN for the row where the key was missing. Every column still ends up the same length, that row simply gets a missing value in that one spot.

blocks.text: 3.3 From a 2D NumPy Array Plus Column Names

Remember from the NumPy module that a 2D array is just rows and columns of raw numbers, with no names attached to either axis. A DataFrame is what you get once you hand that raw array some labels. Pass the array as the data and a plain list of strings as the columns argument, and pandas wraps the whole thing with names.

blocks.alt: A raw 2D NumPy array being paired with a list of column names to produce a labeled DataFrame
blocks.caption: A NumPy array has no names attached. Column names are what turn it into a DataFrame.

code.content:
import numpy as np

arr = np.array([
    [72000, 5],
    [65000, 3],
    [81000, 7],
])
df = pd.DataFrame(arr, columns=["salary", "years_experience"])
print(df)
#    salary  years_experience
# 0   72000                 5
# 1   65000                 3
# 2   81000                 7

blocks.text: This path is extremely common at the boundary between NumPy heavy code, like a model output or a matrix of computed features, and pandas heavy code, where you want readable column names for inspection and reporting.
4. Two Separate Label Axes

A Series has exactly one axis of labels, its index. A DataFrame has two, and keeping them straight matters a lot once you start doing real work. There is the row index, labeling each row, and there is the column index, labeling each column. Pandas usually just calls the column index the "columns".

blocks.alt: A DataFrame with two separate label axes, a row index and a column index, shown branching off the same table
blocks.caption: A DataFrame carries two label axes, not one, a row index and a column index.

code.content:
print(df.index)     # the row axis, RangeIndex(start=0, stop=3, step=1)
print(df.columns)   # the column axis, Index(["salary", "years_experience"], dtype="object")

blocks.title: The upgrade from Series to DataFrame in one sentence
blocks.content: A Series has one labeled axis. A DataFrame has two. Almost every DataFrame method you learn from here on takes an axis argument precisely because there are now two directions to choose between.

blocks.text: 5. Selecting Columns

Pulling data out of a DataFrame by column name is something you will do dozens of times a day. The exact syntax you use, single brackets or double brackets, changes what type of object you get back, and mixing this up is one of the most common early pandas mistakes.
5.1 A Single Column Returns a Series
Index a DataFrame with one column name, in single brackets, and you get back a Series. This is the same idea as pulling one Series out of the dict of Series mental model from earlier in this lesson.
5.2 Multiple Columns Return a DataFrame
Pass a list of column names instead of a single name, which means an extra pair of brackets, and you get back a DataFrame, not a Series, even if that list only has one name in it.

blocks.alt: Single bracket column selection on a DataFrame returning a Series, contrasted with double bracket selection returning a DataFrame
blocks.caption: One bracket gets you a Series. Two brackets get you a DataFrame, even a one column one.

blocks.title: The classic double bracket confusion
blocks.content: df["salary"] and df[["salary"]] look nearly identical but return two different types of object. The first is a Series, the second is a single column DataFrame. If you ever get a confusing error about a Series not having some DataFrame method, or the reverse, check whether you meant single brackets or double brackets. This single detail trips up almost every pandas beginner at least once.

blocks.text: 6. Adding and Dropping Columns
Because a DataFrame is a dict of Series under the hood, adding and removing columns feels a lot like adding and removing keys from a dict.
6.1 Adding a New Column
Assign to a new column name in bracket notation and pandas creates that column for you, aligned automatically against the shared row index.

blocks.alt: A three column DataFrame gaining a new bonus column, becoming a four column DataFrame
blocks.caption: Assigning to a new column name adds it, aligned to the existing row index.

code.content:
df["bonus"] = df["salary"] * 0.10
print(df)
#    salary  years_experience   bonus
# 0   72000                 5  7200.0
# 1   65000                 3  6500.0
# 2   81000                 7  8100.0

blocks.text: Notice that the new column was computed directly from an existing one using ordinary arithmetic. That works because df["salary"] is a Series, and Series support fast, vectorized math, exactly like you learned with NumPy arrays.
6.2 Dropping a Column

Use .drop() with columns= to remove one or more columns. By default this returns a new DataFrame rather than changing the original in place, so remember to reassign it, or pass inplace=True if you really want to mutate the original.

blocks.alt: A four column DataFrame dropping its department column and becoming a three column DataFrame
blocks.caption: Dropping a column removes it from the column axis, the row index is untouched.

blocks.text: 7. A Quick Preview of Row Selection

You have only seen column selection so far, but you will need to grab rows constantly too. A full lesson on this is coming later in the module, so treat this as just enough to get you moving, not the complete picture.

items: .loc[] selects rows and columns by their labels, the actual index values and column names.
.iloc[] selects rows and columns by their plain integer position, ignoring labels entirely.

code.content:
print(df.loc[0])          # the row labeled 0, by index label
print(df.iloc[0])         # the first row, by position, same result here

print(df.loc[0, "salary"])   # single cell, by label
print(df.iloc[0, 0])         # single cell, by position

blocks.title: Why both exist
blocks.content: When the row index is just the default 0, 1, 2, positions and labels line up so .loc and .iloc look interchangeable. Once a DataFrame has a custom index, like employee IDs or dates, they diverge fast. Keep the distinction filed away, the dedicated lesson will drill into it properly.

blocks.text: 8. The Axis Parameter on a DataFrame

You met the axis parameter back in the NumPy statistical operations lesson, where axis 0 collapsed down the rows and axis 1 collapsed across the columns of a 2D array. That exact same rule carries over to a DataFrame unchanged, because a DataFrame is really just a labeled 2D array underneath.
8.1 axis=0, Down the Rows, Per Column

With axis=0, pandas walks down each column, one column at a time, and gives you back one result per column. This is also the default for most aggregate methods, so you often do not even need to type it.

blocks.alt: axis equals 0 collapsing down the rows of a DataFrame and producing one result per column
blocks.caption: axis 0 walks down the rows, so what survives is one number per column.

blocks.text: 8.2 axis=1, Across the Columns, Per Row
With axis=1, pandas instead walks across each row, one row at a time, and gives you back one result per row.

blocks.alt: axis equals 1 collapsing across the columns of a DataFrame and producing one result per row
blocks.caption: axis 1 walks across the columns, so what survives is one number per row.

blocks.title: The one line memory trick
blocks.content: The axis you name is the one that disappears. Name axis 0 and the rows disappear, leaving one value per column. Name axis 1 and the columns disappear, leaving one value per row. This is exactly the same rule you already learned for NumPy arrays, nothing new to memorize here.

blocks.text: 9. Worked Example: An Employees DataFrame
Time to put every piece from this lesson together on one small, realistic table: a handful of employees with a name, a department, and a salary.
9.1 Building the DataFrame

code.content:
import pandas as pd

employees = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Asha", "Rohit", "Meera", "Karan", "Divya"],
    "department": ["Engineering", "Sales", "Engineering", "Sales", "Engineering"],
    "salary": [72000, 65000, 81000, 68000, 77000],
})
print(employees)
#     name   department  salary
# 0   Asha  Engineering   72000
# 1  Rohit        Sales   65000
# 2  Meera  Engineering   81000
# 3  Karan        Sales   68000
# 4  Divya  Engineering   77000

blocks.alt: A worked employees DataFrame with name, department, and salary columns, then a computed bonus column, then a department average
blocks.caption: The full worked example: build the table, add a computed column, then aggregate by department.

blocks.text: 9.2 Selecting and Computing a New Column

First, grab just the salary column as a Series, and separately grab name and salary together as a small DataFrame, to see the single versus double bracket difference from earlier in action on real data.

code.content:
salary_series = employees["salary"]
print(type(salary_series))   # Series

name_salary_df = employees[["name", "salary"]]
print(type(name_salary_df))  # DataFrame

blocks.text: Now add a computed column, a 10 percent bonus, using ordinary vectorized arithmetic on the salary Series.

code.content:
employees["bonus"] = employees["salary"] * 0.10
print(employees[["name", "salary", "bonus"]])
#     name  salary   bonus
# 0   Asha   72000  7200.0
# 1  Rohit   65000  6500.0
# 2  Meera   81000  8100.0
# 3  Karan   68000  6800.0
# 4  Divya   77000  7700.0

blocks.text: 9.3 A Simple Aggregate by Department

Finally, a quick aggregate: the average salary for each department. This peeks slightly ahead at groupby, which gets its own full lesson soon, but it is a satisfying way to see the whole DataFrame come together.

code.content:
avg_by_dept = employees.groupby("department")["salary"].mean()
print(avg_by_dept)
# department
# Engineering    76666.67
# Sales          66500.00
# Name: salary, dtype: float64

blocks.text: Every idea from this lesson shows up in that one short block of code: a shared row index holding it all together, single bracket column selection returning a Series, a computed column added with plain arithmetic, and an aggregate that collapses rows down into a per group summary, the same axis 0 style collapsing you just studied, just grouped first.
10. Recap

items: A DataFrame is a dict of Series that all share one common row index, each column is genuinely a Series.
Build one from a dict of lists, keys become columns, or from a list of dicts, each dict becomes a row, or from a 2D NumPy array plus a list of column names.
A DataFrame carries two label axes, a row index and a column index, unlike a Series which only has one.
df["col"] with single brackets returns a Series, df[["c1", "c2"]] with double brackets returns a DataFrame, even for one column.
New columns are assigned directly, columns are removed with .drop(columns=...).
.loc and .iloc give you a first taste of row selection, by label and by position, with the full lesson still to come.
axis=0 collapses down the rows for a per column result, axis=1 collapses across the columns for a per row result, exactly like the axis rule you learned in NumPy.

blocks.text: You now have the core mental model for the DataFrame, the object you will spend the rest of this module reading data into, filtering, sorting, cleaning, and reshaping. Every upcoming lesson builds directly on top of what you just learned here.
